commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList, Deadline, Event, and LittleR rely on several assumptions
that their own logic guarantees but that were previously
undocumented and unenforced, e.g. that checkIndex() validates bounds
before an index is used, that Parser only ever produces non-null
dates before Deadline/Event are constructed, and that TaskList.add()
appends new tasks to the end of the list.

Without an explicit check, a future refactor could silently break
one of these assumptions and cause confusing bugs far from their
root cause, e.g. the wrong task shown in a confirmation message, or
a NullPointerException several calls downstream.

Let's add assert statements at each of these points to document the
assumptions and fail fast during development/testing if any of them
is ever violated. Since assertions are disabled by default at
runtime, this adds zero overhead or risk for real users; the checks
only run when explicitly enabled, e.g. via -ea or Gradle's test task.

Assertions are only used for conditions guaranteed by our own code's
logic, not for validating user input, which continues to be handled
via LittleRException as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.task package: improve code quality
commitResults.messageBody:
Todo, Deadline, and Event hardcode their storage type codes ("T",
"D", "E") as magic literals inside toFileString(). Deadline's due
field and Event's from/to fields are assigned once in the
constructor but are not marked final, so their immutability is only
an implicit assumption. Event's from/to field names are prepositions
rather than nouns and don't explain what they represent on their
own. Event.isOccurringOn() also combines up to four comparison
sub-conditions into a single compound boolean expression across two
branches, which is hard to read at a glance.

Left as-is, these reduce readability and make future changes riskier
(e.g. renaming a type code wouldn't surface every usage site, and
a reader has to check every method in Deadline/Event to confirm a
field is never mutated.)

Let's, for the littler.task package:
* introduce a private static final TYPE_CODE constant in Todo,
  Deadline, and Event instead of inline type-code strings
* mark Deadline.due and Event.from/to as final
* rename Event's from/to fields to startDateTime/endDateTime
* extract each sub-condition in Event.isOccurringOn() into a named
  intermediate boolean, replacing the single compound expression

These changes follow the Avoid Magic Numbers, Make the Code Obvious,
Use Nouns for Things, Use Name to Explain, and Avoid Complicated
Expressions guidelines from the course's Code Quality chapter. No
behavior is changed -- Event.isOccurringOn()'s evaluated logic is
identical, only its structure is clearer.

Note: Storage.parseLine() still hardcodes "T"/"D"/"E" on the reading
side, duplicating the same literals introduced as constants here.
Left untouched for now since Storage will be reviewed in a separate
pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.task, littler.storage: remove duplicated type-code text
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage.java has the letters "T", "D", and "E" typed directly into
it to check what kind of task a saved line represents. But we just
gave Todo, Deadline, and Event their own named constants for these
same letters. So now the same information (which letter means which
task type) exists in two separate places, and nothing stops them
from going out of sync if one is ever changed without the other.

Storage.java also uses a try/catch to figure out if a saved line is
missing a date. This works, but it's not clear just from reading it,
you have to already know that accessing a missing array position
is what causes the error being caught. It would be clearer to just
check directly whether the date is there.

Let's:
* make each TYPE_CODE constant public, so Storage can use them
  directly instead of typing the letters again
* replace the hardcoded "T"/"D"/"E" checks in Storage with
  Todo.TYPE_CODE / Deadline.TYPE_CODE / Event.TYPE_CODE
* replace the try/catch with a direct check on how many fields the
  line has, so it's obvious what's actually being checked

This makes the code easier to read and removes a spot where the two
files could quietly fall out of sync with each other.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.command package: improve code quality
commitResults.messageBody:
Parser.parseTask() was handling three different task types
(deadline, event, todo) all inside one method, mixing the general
"figure out which type this is" logic with the specific details of
each type. This made the method longer and harder to read at a
glance than it needed to be.

The text used to recognize deadline/event input ("/by", "/from",
"/to") also lived in Parser.java, even though each delimiter only
makes sense for one specific task type. Deadline and Event already
store their own TYPE_CODE for how they're written to the save file,
so this split the knowledge about a task type across two different
classes (how it's recognized from input, and how it's saved to
disk).

On top of that, parseEvent() combined the from/to delimiters using
split(), which treats its input as a pattern for matching text (a
"regex"), not as plain text. This happened to work only because
"/from" and "/to" don't contain any characters with a special
meaning in that pattern language. Nothing in the code actually
guaranteed that, so a future delimiter change could quietly break it
without an obvious error.

Command.java's class comment was also missing the usual space before
each line's *, so it didn't match the rest of the codebase's style.

Let's:
* split parseTask() into three small private methods, one per task
  type, so each one is easier to read on its own
* move each delimiter ("/by", "/from", "/to") into the task class it
  belongs to (Deadline, Event), as a public constant, the same way
  TYPE_CODE already works -- Parser now reads these instead of
  hardcoding them
* wrap the delimiters with Pattern.quote() when splitting, so
  split() treats them as plain text no matter what characters they
  contain, instead of relying on them staying "safe" by coincidence
* fix the spacing in Command.java's class comment to match the rest
  of the file

No behavior changes and the same input formats, task creation, and
error messages still apply.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.datetime package: improve code quality
commitResults.messageBody:
toStorageString() and fromStorageString() use the text "|" and
"NONE" directly in the code, with nothing showing that both methods
need to agree on what these mean. fromStorageString() also splits on
"|" using split(), which treats its input as a pattern for matching
text, not plain text. This is the same kind of problem we fixed
in Parser for the event delimiters.

compareDate() and compareTime() also rebuild, by hand, comparison
logic that LocalDate and LocalTime already provide (they can compare
themselves directly). Writing this out manually with if/else is more
code than needed for something the language already does correctly.

Let's:
* turn "|" and "NONE" into named constants (STORAGE_DELIMITER,
  NO_TIME_MARKER) used by both methods, so they can't drift apart
* use Pattern.quote() when splitting on the delimiter, so it's
  always treated as plain text, matching how we handle this in
  Parser
* replace the manual if/else comparison logic in compareDate() and
  compareTime() with a direct call to LocalDate/LocalTime's own
  comparison, wrapped in Integer.signum() to keep returning exactly
  -1, 0, or 1 as before

No behavior changes, dates and times are still stored, read back,
and compared exactly the same way as before.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.ui: remove duplicated task-line formatting
commitResults.messageBody:
taskList() builds each numbered line by hand:

    (i + 1) + ". " + tasks.get(i)

even though taskWithIndex() already exists to do exactly this. Two
different places now define what a numbered task line looks like,
so if that format ever changes, it's easy to update one and forget
the other.

Let's have taskList() call taskWithIndex() instead of repeating the
same formatting logic.

No behavior changes. The printed output is identical to before.

commitResults.messageTitle: LittleR: fix silent error reporting and duplicate save on exit
commitResults.messageBody:
UI.error() formats and returns an error message -- it does not print
anything. Both the constructor (when loading fails) and
saveQuietly() (when saving fails) called UI.error() and discarded
the result, so the code looked like it was reporting an error but
the user never actually saw one. Load/save failures were failing
completely silently.

Separately, every call to converse() already saves the task list
right before returning, but the EXIT case also called saveQuietly()
explicitly beforehand, causing an extra, unnecessary save every time
the user exits.

printMatchingTasks() and printTasksOnDate() also each contained the
same loop for turning a list of matching tasks into numbered lines
of output.

Let's:
* have the constructor print the load error message instead of
  discarding it
* have saveQuietly() return the formatted error message (or an
  empty string on success) so converse() can actually include it in
  the output shown to the user
* remove the redundant explicit save in the EXIT case, relying on
  the single save that already runs after every command
* extract the repeated numbering loop into a shared
  appendTaskLines() helper
* remove a few comments above switch cases that only restated the
  case label itself (e.g. "// Exit" above "case EXIT:")

Behavior change: load/save failures are now actually shown to the
user instead of being silently swallowed. Everything else is
unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: littler.gui: name magic numbers and shrink variable scope
commitResults.messageBody:
MainWindow used the numbers 1.5 and 2.5 directly when setting up
timers, with nothing explaining what they meant or why those exact
values were chosen. Main.java also had the save file path
"./data/littler.txt" typed directly into the code the same way.

MainWindow also created a PauseTransition called closeDelay at the
very top of handleUserInput(), even though it's only actually used
later, inside the "if the user typed bye" check. This means an
unused object was being created every single time the user sent any
message, not just when exiting.

Let's:
* give the two timer numbers and the file path proper names
  (REPLY_DELAY_SECONDS, WINDOW_CLOSE_DELAY_SECONDS, DATA_FILE_PATH)
  so it's clear what each one is for
* move the creation of closeDelay inside the "if exiting" block,
  since that's the only place it's used

No behavior changes. The app still waits the same amount of time
before replying and before closing, and still saves to the same
file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use Streams where it improves clarity
commitResults.messageBody:
Several methods manually looped over a list to either filter it down
to matching items or transform each item into something else:

* TaskList.getTasksOn() looped to collect tasks matching a date
* TaskList.findByKeyword() looped to collect tasks matching a keyword
* Storage.save() looped to convert each task into its file-string form
* Command.fromInput() looped to find the first matching command

Each of these is a plain "filter" or "transform" operation over an
existing collection, which the Streams API expresses directly and
concisely.

Let's rewrite each of these using Java Streams:
* getTasksOn() and findByKeyword() now filter the task list and
  collect the results directly into a new ArrayList
* save() now maps each task to its file-string form before writing
* fromInput() now filters for a matching command and returns the
  first one found, or null if none match

Storage.load() was deliberately left as a regular loop, since it
needs to catch and skip per-line errors individually, which doesn't
translate cleanly into a stream without making the code harder to
follow. The task-numbering loops in UI and LittleR were also left
as-is, since they rely on the loop index and build output through
side effects rather than transforming a collection into a new one.

No behavior changes. The same tasks are returned, saved, and
matched as before.
